question: A typeface with small strokes on the ends of its letters is:
option_a: Serif

question: A typeface with no strokes on the ends of its letters is:
option_a: Sans serif

question: Pairing a bold slab headline with a light sans body works because the two are:
option_a: Clearly different from each other, so the reader knows which to read first

question: A poster using four different decorative typefaces most likely looks:
option_a: Chaotic, because nothing establishes an order to read in

question: For a long block of small fine print, the most appropriate choice is:
option_a: A simple, highly legible typeface at a readable size
option_d: A face with very thin strokes

question: The weight of a typeface refers to:
option_a: How thick or thin its strokes are
option_c: How much space it takes up

question: Hierarchy in a design is:
option_a: The order in which a viewer notices things
option_c: The file size of the design

question: A design where every element is the same size has:
option_a: No clear hierarchy, so the viewer does not know where to look first

question: The squint test is used to check:
option_a: Whether the most important element still stands out when detail disappears
option_d: Whether the text is spelled correctly

question: Medium gray text on a busy photograph is hard to read. The most effective single fix is:
option_a: Increase the contrast between the text and what is behind it

question: Contrast, in design, means:
option_a: A difference that makes one thing stand out from another

question: Proximity is the principle that:
option_a: Related things are placed near each other and unrelated things apart

question: Whitespace is:
option_a: Empty space used on purpose
option_b: Space that was left over by mistake
option_d: Wasted area that should be filled

question: Alignment in a layout means:
option_a: Edges lining up on purpose

question: A layout where some elements are centered and others are left aligned usually looks:
option_a: Unintentional, because the eye notices the inconsistent edges

question: A focal point is:
option_a: The element a viewer is meant to notice first

question: You are exporting a poster to hand in and to put on a website. The right pair is:
option_a: A PDF to submit and a PNG or JPG to display online

question: Delivering an editable project file instead of an exported image is a problem because:
option_a: The recipient may not have the software or fonts to open it correctly
option_b: Project files are always too small

question: UX stands for:
option_a: User experience

question: UI stands for:
option_a: User interface

question: The difference between UX and UI is best described as:
option_a: UX is how it feels to use something, UI is the actual screens and controls
option_b: UX is for phones and UI is for computers
option_c: They are two names for the same thing
option_d: UI comes first and UX comes after

question: Good UI with bad UX describes a product that is:
option_a: Attractive but hard to actually use

question: A wireframe is:
option_a: A low-detail sketch of a screen's structure, using boxes and labels

question: Wireframes are made before finished visuals because:
option_a: It is much cheaper to be wrong on paper than after something is built
option_c: Color takes too long to choose

question: A prototype is:
option_a: A rough, connected version used to test whether something works
option_c: A written description of a design

question: A user journey is:
option_a: The path a person takes through a product to get what they need
option_c: The order pages were designed in
option_d: How long a person stays on a site

question: A tab bar is:
option_a: A row of a few destinations pinned to the bottom of a screen
option_b: A menu hidden behind three lines

question: By convention, a back button belongs:
option_a: In the top left, in the same place on every screen

question: Breaking a well-known convention, like moving the back button, costs you because:
option_a: Every person using the product pays a small amount of attention on every screen
option_b: It is technically harder to build

question: How many primary actions should a screen have?
option_a: One

question: Which is NOT a reliable way to make a primary action stand out?
option_a: Placing it wherever there happens to be room
option_b: Making it larger than what is near it
option_c: Giving it the only saturated color on the screen

question: An empty state is:
option_a: What a screen shows when there is nothing in it yet
option_b: A screen that failed to load
option_c: A blank page left in by mistake

question: An empty state should:
option_a: Say what goes here and how to add the first one

question: A modal, or dialog, is best used to:
option_a: Confirm something important before continuing

question: Showing a loading state matters because:
option_a: A screen where nothing appears to be happening reads as broken
option_c: It is required by app stores

question: A list of twenty items on a phone screen should:
option_a: Scroll, with rows at a readable size
option_b: Shrink so all twenty fit at once

question: In a design tool, a component is:
option_a: A master copy, where changing the master updates every instance

question: The main reason to make a repeated navigation bar into a component is:
option_a: You change it once instead of fixing the same thing on every screen
option_d: It prevents others from editing it

question: Placeholder text in an empty input field should be:
option_a: Gray, and an example of what goes there
option_b: The same color as typed text

question: When testing a prototype on another person, the designer should:
option_a: Give them the task and then say nothing
option_b: Explain each screen as they go
option_d: Ask whether they like the colors

question: During a user test, every time the designer wants to explain something, it means:
option_a: They have found a design problem
option_b: The tester is not paying attention

question: Scoping a project to one task a person does is useful because:
option_a: A small thing finished well is more valuable than a large thing left vague
option_b: Clients pay more for small projects
